lead: A MOSFET is a capacitor taught to conduct. A gate on a thin oxide above doped silicon first pushes the majority carriers away from the surface, then pulls minority carriers into a thin channel. A source and a drain let current flow along that channel. Whether the channel is absent, continuous or pinched off gives the three regions: cutoff, linear and saturation. Every current, delay and power formula in VLSI starts by naming the region.

sections.h3: The MOS capacitor: accumulation, depletion and inversion

blocks.text: Take a p-type body with acceptor doping N<sub>A</sub> (cm⁻³), so holes are the majority carriers. Silicon dioxide of thickness t<sub>ox</sub>, a few nanometres, covers it, and a metal or polysilicon gate sits on top. This is a parallel-plate capacitor with C<sub>ox</sub> = ε<sub>ox</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub> per unit area, where ε<sub>ox</sub> ≈ 3.45 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m.
The flat-band voltage V<sub>FB</sub> is the gate-to-body voltage at which the surface holds no net charge. Three states follow as the gate voltage V<sub>G</sub> rises.

items: Accumulation (VG < VFB). The negative gate charge attracts holes, which pile up at the surface.
Depletion (VG a little above VFB). The positive gate repels holes, leaving a depletion region of width Wd that holds only fixed acceptor ions. The band bending at the surface, φs, grows with VG.

Inversion (φs ≥ 2φF). Electrons, the minority carriers, are drawn to the surface. At φs = 2φF the surface electron density equals the bulk hole density: the surface has turned n-type, and this layer is the channel. Here φF = (kT/q) ln(NA/ni) is the bulk Fermi potential and ni ≈ 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³.

blocks.text: The capacitance-voltage (C-V) curve shows the same states. In accumulation C = Cox. In depletion a depletion capacitance Cdep adds in series, so C = CoxCdep/(Cox + Cdep) dips to a minimum near threshold. In inversion C returns to Cox at low frequency; at high frequency the electrons cannot follow and C stays low. The gate voltage where strong inversion begins is the threshold voltage VT (see Threshold voltage and body effect).

sections.h3: From capacitor to transistor: the channel and pinch-off

blocks.text: Add n⁺ source (S) and drain (D) regions on either side of the gate (G); with the body (B) the device has four terminals. In an nMOS the source is the lower-voltage terminal, usually tied to the body at ground.

With V<sub>DS</sub> = 0 and V<sub>GS</sub> > V<sub>T</sub>, a uniform channel joins source and drain. The overdrive V<sub>ov</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> sets its charge per unit area, Q<sub>I</sub> ≈ C<sub>ox</sub>·V<sub>ov</sub>.

Now raise VDS. The channel potential V(x) rises from 0 at the source to VDS at the drain, so the local charge Cox[VGS − V(x) − VT] is largest at the source and smallest at the drain. When VDS = VGS − VT the drain-end charge falls to zero: the channel is pinched off. Extra drain voltage drops across a short depleted gap; electrons are swept across it, so the current stays nearly constant.

sections.h3: The three regions of nMOS and pMOS

blocks.text: Cutoff: no channel, only leakage (see Leakage and subthreshold conduction). Linear (triode or ohmic): a continuous channel, a gate-controlled resistor. Saturation: pinched off at the drain, a current source set by VGS.

A pMOS is the mirror image: n-type body (an n-well in CMOS), p⁺ source and drain, a hole channel. Its source is the higher-voltage terminal, so V<sub>GS</sub>, V<sub>DS</sub> and V<sub>Tp</sub> are negative. Use V<sub>SG</sub> = V<sub>S</sub> − V<sub>G</sub> and V<sub>SD</sub> = V<sub>S</sub> − V<sub>D</sub>, positive when it conducts, and compare them with |V<sub>Tp</sub>|.

blocks.text: Some syllabi speak of characteristics "under static and dynamic conditions": static is the DC behaviour in these regions (I-V characteristics); dynamic is the charging of the device capacitances (capacitances and parasitic resistances).

In logic a transistor is a switch. An nMOS turns on with a high gate; it passes a strong 0 but only a weak 1 (V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>Tn</sub>), because it turns off once V<sub>GS</sub> falls to V<sub>Tn</sub>. A pMOS turns on with a low gate and passes a strong 1 but a weak 0.

NMOS logic pulls the output down with nMOS transistors and up with a load (a resistor or depletion-mode nMOS); while the output is low, current flows through the load all the time. CMOS logic pairs each pull-down nMOS network with a complementary pull-up pMOS network on the same inputs, so in any steady state one network is off and almost no static current flows. Load types and inverter curves belong to the topics NMOS inverters and CMOS inverter DC characteristics.

examples.question: A CMOS inverter runs from V<sub>DD</sub> = 1.8 V with V<sub>Tn</sub> = 0.5 V and V<sub>Tp</sub> = −0.5 V. At one instant V<sub>in</sub> = 0.8 V and V<sub>out</sub> = 1.5 V. The nMOS source is at ground and the pMOS source at V<sub>DD</sub>. Name the region of each transistor.
steps: nMOS: V<sub>GS</sub> = 0.8 V ≥ 0.5 V, so a channel exists; overdrive = 0.8 − 0.5 = 0.3 V.
VDS = 1.5 V ≥ 0.3 V, so the drain end is pinched off: saturation.
pMOS: V<sub>SG</sub> = 1.8 − 0.8 = 1.0 V ≥ 0.5 V, so a hole channel exists; overdrive = 0.5 V.
VSD = 1.8 − 1.5 = 0.3 V < 0.5 V, so the channel is continuous: linear.

examples.question: An nMOS has V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V and C<sub>ox</sub> = 8.6 fF/µm², with V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.4 V. Find the channel charge per µm² at the source and drain ends, the number of electrons per µm² at the source end, and the V<sub>DS</sub> that pinches the channel off.
steps: Source end: local overdrive = 1.5 − 0 − 0.5 = 1.0 V; charge = 8.6 fF/µm² × 1.0 V = 8.6 fC/µm².
Drain end: local overdrive = 1.5 − 0.4 − 0.5 = 0.6 V; charge = 8.6 × 0.6 = 5.16 fC/µm², 40 % less.
Electrons at the source end: 8.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ C ÷ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = 5.4 × 10⁴ per µm².
Pinch-off when the drain-end overdrive is zero: V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> = 1.0 V.
examples.answer: 8.6 fC/µm² at the source, 5.16 fC/µm² at the drain, about 54 000 electrons per µm² at the source, pinch-off at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 V.

traps: For a p-type body, accumulation is below flat band (V<sub>G</sub> < V<sub>FB</sub>); above V<sub>FB</sub> comes depletion, then inversion.
Compare the full V<sub>DS</sub> with V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>. Do not subtract the overdrive from V<sub>DS</sub> first.
For a pMOS compare V<sub>SG</sub> with |V<sub>Tp</sub>| and V<sub>SD</sub> with V<sub>SG</sub> − |V<sub>Tp</sub>|; mixing a negative V<sub>GS</sub> with a positive threshold gives the wrong region.
Pinch-off does not stop the current: only the drain end of the channel vanishes.
An nMOS passes a weak 1 (V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>Tn</sub>), a pMOS a weak 0.

quiz.q: Name the three states of a MOS capacitor on a p-type body as V<sub>G</sub> rises from below V<sub>FB</sub>, with the condition for each.
quiz.a: Accumulation, V<sub>G</sub> < V<sub>FB</sub> (holes at the surface); depletion, V<sub>G</sub> just above V<sub>FB</sub> (ionised acceptors, width W<sub>d</sub>); inversion, φ<sub>s</sub> ≥ 2φ<sub>F</sub> (electron layer).

quiz.q: Why does inversion begin at φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub> and not φ<sub>F</sub>?
quiz.a: Bending by φ<sub>F</sub> makes the surface intrinsic; a further φ<sub>F</sub> raises the surface electron density to N<sub>A</sub>, equal to the bulk hole density, which defines strong inversion.

quiz.q: Why does a CMOS gate draw almost no static current while an NMOS gate with a load does?
quiz.a: In CMOS one of the two complementary networks is off in every steady state, so there is no path from V<sub>DD</sub> to ground. The NMOS load is always on, so current flows whenever the output is low.

quiz.q: A pMOS with V<sub>Tp</sub> = −0.5 V has its source at 1.2 V, gate at 0 V and drain at 0.9 V. Which region is it in?
quiz.a: V<sub>SG</sub> = 1.2 V ≥ 0.5 V; overdrive 0.7 V. V<sub>SD</sub> = 0.3 V < 0.7 V, so linear.

quiz.q: An nMOS pass transistor (V<sub>Tn</sub> = 0.5 V) has its gate at 1.8 V and charges a capacitor from 0 V towards a 1.8 V input. Where does the capacitor stop, and why?
quiz.a: The capacitor side is the source. The transistor turns off when V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.8 − V<sub>out</sub> falls to 0.5 V, so the capacitor stops near 1.3 V (lower still with body effect): a weak 1.

beyond: Simulators use compact models such as BSIM and EKV that describe the channel charge smoothly from weak to strong inversion. In fins and nanosheets the same two questions still decide the region: has the gate inverted the surface, and is the drain end pinched off?

figure.caption: The nMOS of worked example 2 at V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.4 V. The electron channel is thickest at the source, where the local overdrive is 1.0 V, and thinner at the drain, where only 0.6 V is left; at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 V the drain end pinches off.
